biography.currentRole: Attorney, private practice (Galveston, TX) — trial and mediation law, full-time while campaigning
priorRoles: Galveston City Council member and Mayor Pro Tem (prior to mayorship)
Texas State Senate District 11 candidate (2008, unsuccessful)

biography.education: B.A. in Spanish Literature, Davidson College (1984); J.D., University of Texas School of Law (1991)
biography.background: Third-generation Texas trial attorney with 30+ years of full-time legal practice focused on mediation, civil litigation, and municipal matters. Grandson of Leon Jaworski, Watergate Special Prosecutor — family legacy of 'no one is above the law' is central to his campaign identity. As Galveston mayor, oversaw post-Hurricane Ike recovery, including politically costly support for rebuilding public housing as mixed-income development — lost re-election in 2012 over this stance. Lost 2022 Democratic AG primary runoff to Rochelle Garza 37%-63%. Now running against state Sen. Nathan Johnson and former FBI agent Tony Box in the 2026 primary. Self-describes as 'the progressive candidate.'
biography.electoralContext: $250K cash on hand as of research date. Polling at approximately 22% in a close three-way Democratic primary. Endorsed by Jolt Action (in the organization's first-ever official primary endorsement), 46 clubs/organizations, and 140+ individual leaders statewide. Texas AFL-CIO endorsed rival Nathan Johnson in 2026 (had endorsed Jaworski in 2022).

statedPositions.quote: Replace Ken Paxton's voter suppression unit with a Voter Enhancement Division; stop voter harassment; enforce laws that expand access like requiring high schools to offer voter registration; prosecute those who suppress votes; interpret election laws to empower voters, not intimidate them; support same-day voter registration, online registration, and making voting by mail more accessible
statedPositions.notes: Core flagship platform commitment, repeated across all outlets and both 2022 and 2026 cycles. Directly within AG's enforcement remit.

statedPositions.quote: Work with School Boards to end vouchers and force the legislature to suitably provide for public education; fight to stop unconstitutional voucher schemes that siphon money from public schools; reversing the privatization of public education; support affordable/free community college and restore in-state tuition for Dreamers
statedPositions.notes: Explicitly anti-voucher; would challenge school vouchers in court via AG litigation power. Also supports Dreamer in-state tuition.

statedPositions.quote: Expand Medicaid to bring billions of federal dollars home, save rural hospitals, and lower local taxes; defend access to affordable care; protect those with pre-existing conditions; oppose cruel restrictions on reproductive health; knock down Paxton's roadblocks to Medicaid; would dismiss Paxton-era ACA lawsuits
statedPositions.notes: Explicit Medicaid expansion support. AG-role framing: use office to remove barriers to health access. Supports ACA; not single-payer advocacy but consistent government-expansion direction.

statedPositions.quote: Legalizing personal use marijuana, ending for-profit prisons, and respecting local decision-making on law enforcement and prosecution; innovative courts that focus on rehabilitation, like mental health and veterans courts; legalizing cannabis achieves criminal justice reform and actually funds the police because we will save $300 million annually when we cease this wasteful, petty prosecution
statedPositions.notes: Consistent across both cycles: marijuana legalization, end for-profit prisons, rehabilitation-focused courts. Frames cannabis decriminalization explicitly as criminal justice reform.

statedPositions.quote: Common-sense gun safety measures that keep kids safe in classrooms and communities; refused support from the gun lobby; believe in responsible gun ownership paired with strong safety standards
statedPositions.notes: Only general statement — no specific measures named (background checks, red flag laws, assault weapons, etc.). Uvalde cited as motivating event in 2022 cycle. No voting record on gun legislation exists. Direction is clearly toward regulation, confidence is low on precise position.

statedPositions.quote: Respect local officials' duties and let them lead; partner with local District Attorneys to prosecute corruption in state political office; supports local decision-making on law enforcement and prosecution
statedPositions.notes: Frames policing via local-control lens and anti-corruption accountability, not explicit 'reform' or 'defund' language. Would not enforce SB8 (bathroom bill) — discretionary non-enforcement on LGBTQ-targeted laws. No history as prosecutor or law enforcement official.

statedPositions.quote: Using science and technology to fight climate change while responsibly managing Texas's energy resources; saving our natural resources (water, land) from for-profit exploitation; join county attorneys to sue polluters
statedPositions.notes: Consistent across both cycles. 'Responsibly managing energy resources' is a hedge that keeps fossil fuel industry in view — not emergency-level climate rhetoric. Concrete action within AG's remit: litigation against polluters.

statedPositions.quote: Division of Affordability focused on helping young adult Texans afford the American Dream: graduating debt free, getting a good job that pays good wages, home ownership or affordable rent and starting a family; limiting the power of billionaires who exert influence over the people's government; stand up for Texas workers by supporting higher wages, protecting the right to organize
statedPositions.notes: AG-specific framing; anti-billionaire populist language. Housing affordability named explicitly. Supports higher wages and union organizing rights; no specific federal safety net program positions stated — not in scope for AG office.

statedPositions.quote: Protect immigrants' constitutional rights; distinguish between immigration and crime; support deploying resources to fight cartel violence while ensuring Dreamers, asylum seekers, and immigrant families are treated with dignity and respect; restore in-state tuition for Dreamers; use OAG budget to fund attorneys to prosecute cartel members; enlist law students to offer legal advice to immigrants seeking asylum; convicting cartel criminals bringing people and drugs over illegally
statedPositions.notes: Distinguishes cartel crime from immigration. Pro-Dreamer, pro-asylum. Pragmatic 'firm immigration partnership with federal government' framing. Not abolish-ICE rhetoric, but clearly pro-immigrant rights.

statedPositions.quote: Abortion is a health care decision that should remain between a woman and her doctor, not politicians; supports returning to the Roe v. Wade standard of care up to fetal viability; opposes Texas's extreme bans rooted in religious ideology; SB8 (Heartbeat Act) is facially unconstitutional; would not criminalize people seeking abortions or abortion providers
statedPositions.notes: Consistent across both cycles. In 2022 runoff, both Democratic finalists explicitly vowed to defend reproductive rights. In 2026, framing retained 'Roe standard up to viability.' SB8 unconstitutionality is a firm legal position. In 2022 he also stated he does not think prosecuting abortion is within the AG's purview — prosecutorial restraint framing.

statedPositions.quote: Create and staff within the OAG a Division of Ethics and Integrity; recruit top-flight attorneys to enhance antitrust and consumer protection enforcement; combine resources with other AGs around the country; pivot the office away from culture wars toward consumer protection; holding private health care insurance companies to account and using AG investigation powers to make them pay health care claims reasonably and on time
statedPositions.notes: Central to his candidacy concept across both cycles. Anti-partisan framing: 'advocate for the people of Texas, rather than a general counsel for a political party.' Specifically names hotel junk fees, health insurance claims enforcement, antitrust.

statedPositions.quote: Create a Division of Ethics and Integrity that will advocate for constitutional amendments and laws providing for term limits, campaign contribution limits, independent redistricting commissions, and citizen-initiated legislation by petition
statedPositions.notes: Structural democracy reform as AG platform — ambitious; would require constitutional amendments. Signals strong anti-corruption/pro-democratic-norms values.

statedPositions.quote: Risked his mayorship to support the rebuilding of Galveston's storm-damaged public housing by championing a community-based solution to build mixed-income housing for thousands, a game-changing first for the Island community — a political choice that made a positive difference for thousands of Island residents but cost him a second term
statedPositions.notes: Tier 4 biographical but exceptionally concrete action: voluntarily sacrificed electoral viability to support public/mixed-income housing for low-income residents. 569 public housing units destroyed by Hurricane Ike. His plan: replace barracks-style projects with mixed-income developments interspersed throughout community. Lost re-election to Lewis Rosen who campaigned against housing plan. Strong signal on housing_affordability_tools and econ_safetynet values.

votingRecord.notes: No legislative voting record exists. Jaworski has never held state or federal legislative office. Municipal mayoral record (Galveston 2010-2012) involves city council-level decisions, not tracked in standard databases. His mayoral record on public housing (see statedPositions above) is the primary action-based evidence. The 2022 AG nomination run and 2026 campaign are the main evidence sources.

keyDecisions.decision: Championed rebuilding Galveston's 569 Hurricane Ike-destroyed public housing units as mixed-income development interspersed throughout community, rather than scattered-site solutions or permanent elimination of public housing stock. Opposed by significant community opposition. HUD ultimately directed Galveston to rebuild. Mixed-income plan approved at Oleander Homes site.
keyDecisions.outcome: New mixed-income housing eventually built; Jaworski lost re-election in 2012 largely over this stance. He has repeatedly cited this as evidence of taking courageous stands at political cost.
keyDecisions.notes: Strongest behavioral evidence in the record. A 2011 recall effort failed (68.6% opposed recall). He lost re-election in 2012. This is the defining evidence for his values on housing_affordability_tools.

keyDecisions.decision: Resolved decades-long financing dispute for Seawall Boulevard improvements via popular election. Improvements included new Seawall Shuttle bus service with stops at 16 intersections between 4th and 81st Streets, bicycle racks at 28 locations, and public restroom facilities funded by parking fee revenues.
keyDecisions.notes: Initiated public transit investment (Seawall Shuttle) and multi-modal infrastructure. Moderate signal toward transit/public investment. Practical governance rather than ideological posture.

positionConflicts.topic: Climate/energy: progressive self-identification vs. hedged energy language
positionConflicts.conflict: Describes himself as 'the progressive candidate' but on climate states 'use science and technology to fight climate change while responsibly managing Texas's energy resources' — language that accommodates continued fossil fuel management. No explicit fossil-fuel phase-out position. This is a notable hedge.
positionConflicts.notes: Texas AG context: the office does not directly regulate energy. This language likely reflects Texas electoral reality and the AG's actual remit rather than a retreat from climate belief. Score toward moderate on climate_energy_portfolio, not at the progressive pole.

positionConflicts.conflict: In 2022 runoff, Jaworski stated he would not prosecute abortion as outside the AG's purview — a more restrained framing than Garza's. His 2026 platform uses stronger language ('oppose cruel restrictions') but the underlying legal theory (prosecutorial restraint) may still shape his approach.
positionConflicts.notes: Not a contradiction — a distinction in approach (legal restraint framing vs. active litigation). Both cycles are clearly pro-choice. Score as clearly pro-access.

positionConflicts.conflict: States 'common-sense gun safety' without naming specific measures. Cannot be scored with high confidence on the justice_firearms axis beyond the general direction.
positionConflicts.notes: Direction is clearly toward regulation; confidence is LOW on precise position. Score toward pole A but with low confidence.

positionConflicts.conflict: Endorsed by Texas AFL-CIO in 2022 but not in 2026 — that endorsement went to Nathan Johnson. His stated workers' rights positions are unchanged; the shift appears to reflect the AFL-CIO's preference for Johnson's legislative background rather than a policy differentiation.
positionConflicts.notes: Does not change the policy position evidence. Noted for context only.

evidenceSummary.notes: Jaworski has no legislative voting record — all evidence is Tier 2-3 (campaign statements, structured interviews, news coverage) plus Tier 4 (mayoral behavioral record). The mayoral public housing decision is the only action-based evidence, and it is strong. His positions have been tested across two full AG campaigns (2022 and 2026), multiple structured Q&As, and a primary debate, giving reasonable confidence that stated 2026 positions are stable. Main scoring consideration: he is running for AG specifically, so his platform is filtered through 'what can the AG do?' — he may hold broader progressive views (e.g., on tax policy) that never surface because they are outside AG scope. Do not infer from silence on non-AG issues. The AG office context constrains fiscal, tax, permitting, and energy axes: these should be scored conservatively or omitted.
